paragraphs.text: DSH 会话太大、加载越来越慢、最后 OOM 打不开？启动时清掉会话日志里没人读的流式碎片：实测 272 MB -> 12 MB，843 万对象 -> 不再撞内存上限，58 -> 238 tok/s。
DeepSeek Harness plugin that deletes dead streaming fragments so the next load is smaller.
# dsh-session-vacuum

> **Topics:** `dsh` · `dsh-plugin` · `deepseek-harness` · `session-cleanup` · `session-log` ·
> `str
eaming-fragments` · `vacuum` · `prune` · `oom` · `long-session` · `memory-optimization`

**Is your DSH session getting slower every turn, slower to load, and eventually unopenable — or

does it just OOM?**

That is not a feeling. Every token is written twice: the fragments (`assistant/chunk` and the
packed

`text-chunks` / `reasoning-chunks` / `tool-call-chunks` rows) are read by nothing, and
they pile up

. A 1,813-turn conversation reached **272 MB on disk**, expanded into **8.43 million
objects** when
loaded, took **1.29 GB resident**, and died.

This plugin deletes them **on disk** — not hidden, actually deleted — so the next load is
smaller be

fore anything else happens. Same session after one pass: **86.67 MB → 16.99 MB**,
169,795 fragments
→ 0, and the non-fragment content: **nothing lost** (`dropped=0`).

**You are accumulating this from turn one.** Measured on real sessions, the number of prunable
fragm

ents tracks output tokens at roughly **0.95–0.99 : 1** — eight sessions, from 88 fragments
for a 91-

token one-turn chat up to 1,498 fragments for a 1,516-token six-turn one. Nothing reads
them; they a

chat up to 1,498 fragments for a 1,516-token six-turn one. Nothing reads
them; they are write-only.

**So you do not have to be in trouble yet.** This is a preventive plugin as much as a rescue one:
in

stall it while the log is still small and the threshold is never crossed. It is not only about
avoid

ing the crash, either — measured across 60 sessions, the median **log-read** speedup after a
pass is

**×7.77** (best ×97.5, scope spelled out below), which is exactly the cost a page refresh
sits on.

Below the thresholds it touches nothing, and a session you are using is never touched at

## Why

A session log is a concatenation of zstd frames holding JSONL rows. Every token a model
streams is w

ritten twice: once as a raw delta (`assistant/chunk`, and the packed rows
`text-chunks` / `reasoning

-chunks` / `tool-call-chunks`) and once inside the finalised
`assistant/message`. **Nothing reads th

e fragments.** Replay does not read them, the model is
never fed them — the projection layer does no

t even know the word `chunks`. They accumulate
because they are write-only.
Measured on the session that motivated this plugin, a 1,813-turn conversation:

| rows in the log | 224,000 |
| file on disk | 272 MB |
| objects after loading it | 8.43 million |

| resident memory while loaded | 1.29 GB |
| outcome | out of memory |

The file is small enough to sit on disk unnoticed and large enough to kill the process that
loads it

. And because every load pays that cost, the session gets slower and eventually
unopenable — while t
he rows that cause it are provably unused.
After a cleanup, on the very same session:
| | before | after |

| session file | 86.67 MB | 16.99 MB |
| fragment rows | 169,795 | 0 |
[该节后续省略]
## Requirements / compatibility

**After installing, confirm it actually works — a profile that boots is not proof.**
A plugin can lo

ad cleanly, serve its routes and still break the host; we have seen exactly
that. So the acceptance

test is: **create a new session and send it one message**, then check
`$DSH_HOME/logs/session-vacuum

.jsonl` for a `run-start` / `run-end` pair about
`startDelayMs` after boot. If new sessions cannot b

e created at all, remove the mount line
above and restart.

Developed and tested against DSH **`0.1.0-rc.7`** — a **customised** build, not a stock
upstream rel

ease. Another version may register its services differently. This plugin declares
`inject: ['tools']

` and uses `ctx.effect`, `ctx.tools.register` (the on-demand tool), and
optionally `ctx.webServer.re
gister` (the preview route).
## Known limitations

- **Frame boundaries come from the frame structure, not from a magic-byte scan.** An earlier
revisio

n of this file sliced each frame up to the next `28 b5 2f fd`. Those four bytes can
occur inside a f

rame's payload; Node's `zstdDecompressSync` does not throw on a mis-sliced
frame (it returns an empt

y buffer), so the cut landed on a clean line boundary and the
*truncated* row set still parsed and s

till passed self-verification — a 661-row synthetic
log was read back as 200 rows and rewritten to 3

8 with status `vacuumed`. The walker now
parses the frame header and every block header, and any byt

es it cannot account for are
reported as `truncated`, which makes `vacuumOne()` return `unreadable-t

ail` and write
nothing. Two regression tests cover it; under the old rule both go red.
- **A session

is not skipped because a `.orig` exists — deliberately.** Skipping on the mere
presence of the back

up would maintain a session only once, because `.orig` is never
removed. Every run re-evaluates the

thresholds instead. The guarantee that does exist:
the first backup is never overwritten.
- **`minIn

tervalMs` does nothing.** Maintenance runs once per boot; there is no second run.
- **A pass is capp

ed at `maxFilesPerRun` files, whichever entry point asks.** The tool does not
get to ignore the cap,

so asking it twice in a row is a way to work through a directory
larger than one pass. The report s

ays how many logs were left by the cap (`not scanned`) so
that count is never silently missing.
- **

One pass at a time.** If a scan is already running, `clean_session_logs` does not queue a
second one

— it says so and does nothing. The log is the record of the pass that is running.
- **Only one file

at a time, and at most `maxFilesPerRun` per boot.** A directory with many
oversized logs is cleaned

up over several restarts.
- **The size fields are rounded to two decimals**, so `beforeMB` and `aft

erMB` are useless for
small logs. They exist for the multi-megabyte ones.
- **It does not and cannot

free memory in the running process.** A session that is already
open stays as large as it is until

it is closed and reopened.
